To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
slow dissociation of an organic anionic chemical from albumin in the liver can reduce the uptake rate of the chemical by the liver.
the dissociation of BSP from albumin in the liver is slow enough that it is a limiting factor in the uptake of BSP.

the strong binding of BSP to albumin, beyond the low dissociation constant, also reduces the uptake of the chemical by the liver due to slow dissociation of the chemical-protein complex in the capillaries.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of in vitro and in silico models to predict the toxicokinetics of organic anions in the liver.
the use of biologically-based modeling to study the kinetics of binding interactions between organic anions such as BSP and albumin.
the development and application of biologically based models of toxicokinetics to predict organ-specific toxicities and to provide guidance in setting safe levels of exposure to chemicals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for the case of BSP and albumin in the isolated, perfused, rat liver system, the slow release of the anion from the albumin protein during passage through sinusoidal capillaries is a significant factor that must be considered in biologically based models of chemical uptake by the liver.
a slow dissociation of BSP from the albumin carrier protein is the primary factor in the reduced uptake of BSP in the liver.
the dissociation of BSP from albumin in the liver is slow and should not be ignored.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in the presence of a slow dissociating organic anion, a biologically-based model that accounts for the kinetics of the anion-protein binding process is necessary for the prediction of uptake in the liver.

the slow dissociation of BSP from albumin, in the presence of high albumin concentrations, is a significant factor that should be considered in the development of biologically-based models of chemical toxicity.

the binding of organic anions to albumin is not just a simple equilibrium process, but also a kinetic process, and the kinetics must be considered in order to predict accurately the uptake of the anion by an organ.
The main takeaway from our work is that
slow dissociation of a drug from its carrier protein can limit uptake and thus reduce the dose of drug available to target tissues.

the slow release of an organic anions bound to albumin may reduce the amount of free anion available for transport across the capillaries, and therefore the amount of anion available to be taken up by an organ.
the dissociation kinetics of organic anions from albumin must be carefully considered when developing biologically-based models for the purpose of predictive toxicology applications.
